newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - S.African Oct CPI seen nudging nine pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - S.African Oct CPI seen nudging nine pct.

text.p: Consumer inflation and trade data next week will provide shaky South African markets with a clearer picture of where inflation will peak this year and the state of the current account, economists said on Friday.

A Reuters poll of eight economists forecast October's consumer price index (CPI), due at 0900 GMT on Wednesday, to gain 8.8 percent year-on-year. That would be the highest level since July 1995 and higher than September's worse-than-expected 8.4 percent year-on-year rate. Month-on-month October CPI was seen up 0.7 percent after a 1.0-percent gain in September.
Economists' forecasts in the Reuter survey ranged from 8.6 to 9.0 percent year-on-year.
October trade data, due from Tuesday onwards, drew a consensus forecast of a 900-million rand surplus compared with a 666.7-million rand surplus in September.
Regarding inflation, continued gains in food prices was seen as the main contributor to higher inflation.
"Food prices will keep on increasing because of the Christmas season although the increase in meat prices is starting to slow down," said Sanlam economist Peter Calitz.
Food inflation jumped 10.4 percent year-on-year in September after August's 7.9-percent increase.
Calitz said a slowdown in food prices and the overall inflation rate would likely not come until the 1997 second half.
Technical factors would also play a part in boosting CPI. Economists noted that CPI rose 6.3 percent year-on-year and 0.3 percent month-on-month in October last year.
They said higher world oil prices and the lagged effects of the rand's depreciation against the dollar since February this year would also weigh on the figure.
A number of periodic surveys, such as reading matter and stationary and hairdressing services and washing prices, would bring further upward pressure on the latest inflation data.

Some consolation for CPI were seen stemming from the 0.25-percentage point cut in the prime rate at the beginning of October, although this was seen partly offset by additional value added tax on financial services.
But looking ahead, economists still predicted a further rise in the inflation number in November.
"However, after November, we're probably going to range-trade between 8.5 percent and 9.5 percent (year-on-year) for the next six months," said Herman van Papendorp of SMK Securities.
Most expected year-on-year consumer inflation to peak between 9.1 to 9.3 percent in November and December.
Though economists were less eager to offer predictions on the trade figure, which is notoriously erratic, those that did venture a forecast were more optimistic than in the past.

"All in all, I'm looking at quite a bullish figure indicating that the (import) volume effect of the weaker exchange rate is starting to come through and that we are starting to see a more synchronised upswing with our major trading partners," said van Papendorp.
Sanlam's Calitz noted that the non-farming sector of the economy was slowing down, especially the manufacturing sector, which would also lead to lower import volumes.
"I'm more optimistic...the current account will still be in deficit, but the trade account should show a much better surplus this time around," he said.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Friday South Africa's economic position was stabilising and the current account deficit would have narrowed sharply in the third quarter.
However, he cautioned that last month's sharp fall in the rand had distorted the situation again.
The Reserve Bank is due to publish its next Quarterly Bulletin containing third quarter data on December 5.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
